critical_operation.description: Bzip2Decoder.decode() handles a whole input buffer in one loop. For each compressed block it allocates an output buffer, inflates the block into it, adds it to the out list and then breaks back into the loop rather than returning. Heap use therefore scales with the total decompressed size of the input buffer rather than with one block, and a small crafted bzip2 stream that decompresses to a very large output can exhaust the heap (CWE-400). The 4.1.68 fix returns after each block so buffers are propagated and released incrementally; its added MAX_BLOCK_LENGTH check is defense-in-depth on top of the existing streamBlockSize bounds, not the reachable defect.

critical_operation.description: complete_io loops until the handshake completes or an error occurs. When the peer sends a ClientHello followed immediately by a close_notify alert, process_new_packets() consumes the alert, leaving is_handshaking() true while wants_read() and wants_write() are both false and eof is still false. None of the return arms at the bottom of the loop match: `(_, true, false)` needs the handshake to be finished, `(true, true, true)` needs eof, so `(..) => {}` falls through and the loop repeats forever, pinning a thread at 100% CPU. The upstream regression test feeds exactly this ClientHello+close_notify byte sequence and expects io::ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof.

critical_operation.description: doGenerate() encodes "." and ".." path segments so a generated URL still resolves to its route after RFC 3986 §5.2.4 dot-segment removal. The encoding uses two strtr() replacements, "/../" -> "/%2E%2E/" and "/./" -> "/%2E/". strtr() consumes the trailing slash of each match, so in a chained sequence such as "../../.." the slash that ends one match is the slash that would start the next; every other segment is left as a literal "." or "..". A URL built from an attacker-controlled route parameter therefore contains unencoded dot segments that strict RFC 3986 consumers (routers, reverse proxies, HTTP clients) remove before percent-decoding, so the URL collapses to a different path than the route intended. The trailing-segment fixup only covers the last segment. The 5.4.53 fix splits the path on / and encodes every dot segment.
